case_study_insert.main_stem: Larkspur Learning Academy (LMA) is a private limited company in the education sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2013 by Daniel Larkspur, it produces tutoring workbooks and online course units for school pupils and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. LMA plans to invest $540,000 in a new e-learning studio, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.00 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. Its tutor numbers have grown quickly as parents seek extra support for their children. LMA faces two problems: tutor absenteeism has reached 7% and complaints about outdated course materials are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Enrolment Report, Term 1 2026: The e-learning pilot delivered 19,000 units last term with a material-error rate of 3.2%, down from 5.1% a year ago. Parent complaints about outdated workbooks fell from 52 to 24 per month. Average query response time is 2.6 days. A survey of 450 parents found 71% would pay up to $0.50 more for regularly updated digital resources and 63% check qualification accreditation before enrolling. Records show 14 of 40 tutors have not completed on-the-job training on the new studio software; accredited training courses cost $620 per tutor.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Larkspur Learning Academy for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has lifted the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, raising the cost of variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will increase by 4.9% from $12.60 to $13.22 per hour, adding to employers' wage bills. (3) Printing paper, broadband and energy input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, education-services inflation stands at 5.6%, and household spending on private tuition grew 3.9% over the same period.

questions.question_text: LMA plans to fund part of its $540,000 e-learning studio with a $300,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for LMA of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no monthly interest or capital repayments, so the $240,000 set aside from earlier profits keeps LMA's cash flow intact while it meets fixed costs of $180,000 a year. With a flat structure and only 40 staff, preserving cash matters because the 11.3% rise in printing, broadband and energy costs would otherwise squeeze the $5.00 contribution on 80,000 units.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids pledging assets as security for the $300,000 loan, so the new e-learning studio cannot be at risk if enrolments fall short. It also leaves Daniel Larkspur's control untouched, since no lender can impose conditions. Retained profit is available immediately with no application delay, letting LMA replace the outdated materials behind rising complaints and invest in the tutor training the business needs. These advantages let LMA focus scarce cash on 7% tutor absenteeism and the 3.2% material-error rate rather than on debt service.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to LMA, its costs, studio and staffing.

questions.question_text: LMA is relaunching its digital resources. Consider advertising in national parenting magazines, sponsoring a school examination board, or targeted social media and email marketing to parents. Which should LMA choose to promote the relaunch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National parenting magazines: Print advertising in national magazines would build broad brand awareness among parents and suit a tutor business aiming to grow enrolment. Production and placement costs are high, however, and readership is nationwide while LMA serves local pupils, so much of the spend misses its market. Results are slow and difficult to attribute to a particular campaign.

Sponsoring a school examination board: This would associate LMA's workbooks with a trusted academic body, supporting the 63% of surveyed parents who check accreditation. It is prestigious but extremely expensive for a 40-staff firm funding a $540,000 studio, and a single sponsorship cannot by itself sell 80,000 units or fix the 3.2% material-error rate.

Targeted social media and email marketing: Direct digital marketing to parents reaches the 71% who would pay $0.50 more for updated resources, can show sample pages instantly, and gives measurable responses at low cost per contact. Messages can be changed quickly as workbooks are revised. The limitation is that parents may ignore unsolicited messages and online claims need credible evidence to be believed. A low cost per contact is especially important for a firm whose fixed costs already run at $180,000 a year.

Recommendation: LMA should choose targeted social media and email marketing, backed by a small accreditation badge on its materials. It reaches the price-responsive 71% and the accreditation-focused 63% far more cheaply than national print, and unlike a one-off sponsorship it can run continuously to support 80,000 units. Magazines are rejected as costly and geographically wasteful; examination-board sponsorship is rejected as unaffordable and unable to deliver sustained volume.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to LMA's survey or product.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of LMA with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options with a justified recommendation that explains why magazines and examination-board sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: LMA has a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership and tutor absenteeism has reached 7%. Explain two benefits for LMA of introducing job enrichment for its tutors.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job enrichment gives the 40 tutors more varied and responsible work, such as designing their own digital resources and checking material accuracy, which satisfies esteem and self-actualisation needs in Maslow's hierarchy. Tutors who own a complete piece of work are more motivated and less likely to take time off, directly tackling the 7% absenteeism rate and improving the 3.2% material-error rate.

Point 2: Enriched jobs let tutors use the new studio software after their on-the-job training, making skills more transferable and reducing the 14 of 40 staff who lack that training. Greater involvement also cuts the $620 per tutor cost of external accredited courses, because experienced staff can mentor others in a flat structure, protecting the $540,000 studio investment while complaints about outdated workbooks fall. Enriched tutors can also cover for the 14 without software training, keeping the 19,000 units on schedule while the $300,000 loan is repaid.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of job enrichment (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to LMA's absenteeism, error rate, training and structure.

questions.question_text: LMA must train 14 of its 40 tutors on the new studio software. Consider on-the-job training or accredited external courses costing $620 per tutor. Which should LMA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning on the studio software keeps the 14 tutors productive and is tailored to LMA's own workbook formats, costing no course fees. That protects the 19,000 units delivered last term and helps reduce the 3.2% material-error rate, since mistakes can be corrected immediately. Drawbacks are that mentor tutors lose some teaching time, inconsistent habits may spread, and there is no external qualification to reassure the 63% of parents who check accreditation.

Accredited external courses: At $620 per tutor, training all 14 costs $8,680 ($620 x 14), manageable against the $540,000 investment. Accreditation supports the 63% of surveyed parents and gives tutors recognised skills. However, it removes 14 of 40 tutors from delivery for a time, worsening the 7% absenteeism pressure, and generic course content may not match LMA's exact studio software, so follow-up coaching would still be required. The $8,680 also competes with the 52 complaints a month about outdated workbooks that need answering during the relaunch, and certification carries an opportunity cost in tutor time.

Decision: LMA should choose on-the-job training first, adding accredited courses for a small number of senior tutors later. It is cheaper, software-specific and avoids losing teaching capacity while absenteeism is 7%; full external training is rejected because the $8,680 and the loss of 14 tutors would disrupt the 80,000-unit plan and the drive to replace outdated materials, and accreditation can be added once the studio is embedded, starting with the tutors who deal most with accreditation-conscious parents and with mentors chosen from the 26 already trained.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to LMA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the benefits and drawbacks of each method in the context of LMA's costs, output and staffing.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and refers to cost, disruption and software relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how LMA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($9.00 − $4.00) = $180,000 ÷ $5.00 = 36,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 36,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.00 − $4.00 = $5.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways LMA's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 36,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 80,000 units to find a margin of safety of 44,000 units (80,000 − 36,000), showing the $540,000 studio can withstand falling enrolments.
2. Use the $5.00 contribution to assess the survey: at 80,000 units a $0.50 premium would add $40,000 (80,000 x $0.50), helping fund the $620 tutor courses.
3. Check that contribution covers fixed costs of $180,000 and interest on the $300,000 loan before expanding, so finance costs do not raise break-even.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $6.25 ($180,000 ÷ 80,000 + $4.00) each term to detect waste from the 3.2% material-error rate and judge whether 11.3% input-cost inflation is absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 36,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: a margin of safety of 44,000 units against 80,000 output; a $0.50 premium adding $40,000; covering $180,000 fixed costs and $300,000 loan interest; and unit-cost benchmarking at $6.25 to track 11.3% input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate LMA's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has LMA's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 13.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 19.5%
ROCE 2025 = 21.5%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $720,000 on revenue of $1,800,000 in 2024 gives 720 ÷ 1,800 = 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $967,000 on $2,150,000 gives 967 ÷ 2,150 = 45.0%. Operating profit of $234,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 13.0% in 2024 and $322,000 ÷ $2,150,000 = 15.0% in 2025. The return on capital employed divides operating profit by capital employed: $234,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 19.5% and $322,000 ÷ $1,500,000 = 21.5%. Cost of sales of $1,080,000 and $1,183,000 reconciles exactly to gross profit in both years.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The move from 40.0% to 45.0% shows more revenue retained after direct costs, as revenue grew $350,000 while cost of sales rose only $103,000, so most of the extra revenue reached gross profit. Operating profitability rose from 13.0% to 15.0%, suggesting the flat structure kept overheads controlled as enrolment grew. The return on capital increased from 19.5% to 21.5%, so the $1,500,000 of capital employed is being used more productively, which supports the $540,000 studio. Interest payable fell from $28,000 to $24,000, reducing the drag on profit.

Conclusion: LMA's financial performance has improved. Every margin rose, the return on capital strengthened and interest payable fell, leaving the business better able to service the $300,000 loan. Management should still address the 7% tutor absenteeism and 3.2% material-error rate, which could undermine these gains.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for LMA of producing regularly updated digital resources.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Updated digital resources match the survey finding that 71% of parents would pay up to $0.50 more and that 63% check accreditation before enrolling. At 80,000 units a $0.50 premium could add $40,000 (80,000 x $0.50), protecting the $5.00 contribution per unit against 11.3% input-cost inflation and helping justify the $540,000 studio and the $300,000 loan that funds it.

Disadvantage: Constantly revising workbooks and online content raises the $4.00 variable cost per unit and needs tutor time, which is scarce with 7% absenteeism and 14 of 40 tutors untrained on the new software. If updates are late, the 3.2% material-error rate and complaints about outdated materials will persist, damaging the accreditation-conscious reputation LMA relies on; late updates would undo the fall from 52 to 24 complaints a month. With no split of the $4.00 variable cost in the insert, the size of the squeeze must remain qualitative, but protecting the $5.00 contribution supports the $540,000 studio investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to LMA's survey data, costs and studio.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in input costs will affect LMA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If LMA's $300,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% x $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 x $300,000), small against fixed costs of $180,000. If the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Parents may also cut discretionary tuition spending when borrowing is dearer, but LMA can largely remove this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (4.9%, to $13.22 an hour): With a workforce of 40 and output of 80,000 units, labour productivity is 80,000 ÷ 40 = 2,000 units per worker. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented; the defensible test is whether each tutor maintains around 2,000 units. With absenteeism at 7%, any fall in productivity would raise unit labour costs and shrink the $5.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (11.3% in paper, broadband and energy): The insert states a variable cost of $4.00 per unit without decomposing it, so only an illustrative bound is possible. If the entire $4.00 rose 11.3%, that is 11.3% x $4.00 = $0.452, about $0.45 per unit; over 80,000 units that is roughly $36,000 a year (80,000 x $0.45). Even a $0.35 rise would cost $28,000 a year (80,000 x $0.35), pulling contribution from $5.00 to about $4.65.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It hits all 80,000 units and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that underpins the $540,000 studio, and at up to about $36,000 a year it far exceeds the conditional $2,250 interest cost. The wage rise is real but cannot be quantified from the insert and depends on the 2,000-unit productivity holding, while interest risk can be fixed. LMA should renegotiate supplier contracts and recover part of the increase through the $0.50 premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to LMA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on LMA's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller, with arithmetic shown from insert figures.
